query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting a minor fraction (≈1–2 at.%) of one base element with tungsten during alloy processing will enhance the mechanical integrity of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy by promoting the formation of finely dispersed tungsten-rich precipitates, while maintaining its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibiting a large caloric effect but poor mechanical integrity and a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Substitute approximately 1–2 atomic percent of one of the base elements with tungsten (W) during the alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied using identical thermal, processing, and loading conditions as the baseline alloy. Caloric and mechanical evaluations are carried out under the same applied-field, pressure, temperature, and compressive loading regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: The tungsten addition is expected to form finely dispersed tungsten-rich precipitates that contribute to grain refinement and improved intergranular cohesion, which in turn enhance crack resistance.
generation.mechanism: W promotes nanoprecipitate formation and microstructural refinement. This microstructural modification improves the alloy’s resistance to crack initiation and propagation without significantly disturbing the phase transformation which is responsible for the caloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement in compressive strength (toward levels reported in previous mechanically reinforced MM′X systems) with the caloric performance remaining within approximately 10% of that of the undoped alloy.
generation.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy characterized by a large caloric response but compromised mechanical integrity leading to cracking under load.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under conditions of applied-field and pressure-field operation, within the temperature range surrounding the caloric phase transition, and under standard compressive loading regimes used in previous studies.
generation.uncertainty: The precise degree of improvement in mechanical integrity and exact retention of caloric performance may vary with processing variations and tungsten concentration, and hence needs experimental confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using identical processing conditions: one set of the pristine (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and one set with 1–2 at.% tungsten substitution. Subject both sets to identical mechanical (compressive strength) testing and caloric response measurements (e.g., isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) under the same applied-field, pressure, and temperature conditions.
measurements: Caloric response (e.g., magnitude of adiabatic temperature change or entropy change under specific field conditions)
Microstructural analysis (to verify tungsten-rich precipitate formation and grain refinement)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in compressive strength (beyond experimental error relative to the baseline) or if their caloric performance deviates by more than ±10% compared to the untreated alloy, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a minor amount of tungsten (W) as a substitutional dopant in the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy will form finely dispersed tungsten-rich precipitates that enhance crack resistance and overall integrity without significantly altering its caloric phase transformation.
drafts.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibiting a large caloric response but poor mechanical integrity leading to cracking.
drafts.intervention: Substitute approximately 1–2 atomic percent of one of the base elements with tungsten (W) during alloy processing.
drafts.conditions: The intervention is applied under identical processing, thermal, and loading conditions as the original alloy, with caloric measurements conducted under the same applied-field, pressure, temperature range, and compressive loading regimes.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of finely dispersed tungsten-rich precipitates and potential grain refinement, which together enhance crack resistance and improve intergranular cohesion.
drafts.mechanism: The tungsten dopant promotes nanoprecipitate formation and may refine the microstructure, increasing the material’s resistance to crack initiation and propagation. This microstructural change is expected to reinforce overall mechanical integrity while leaving the phase transformation responsible for the caloric response largely unperturbed.
drafts.predicted_outcome: An increase in compressive strength toward the range observed in other reinforced MM′X systems (e.g., 150–220 MPa), with the caloric performance (entropy change/temperature change) remaining within approximately 10% of that of the undoped alloy.
drafts.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which has a large caloric effect but suffers from poor integrity and cracking under mechanical load.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis holds under applied-field and pressure-field conditions, within the temperature range surrounding the caloric phase transition, and under typical compressive loading regimes utilized in prior evaluations of both caloric response and mechanical integrity.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: one set of the baseline (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and a second set with 1–2 at.% tungsten substituted. Conduct identical processing treatments and subject both sets to mechanical testing (e.g., compressive strength measurements) as well as caloric property measurements (isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) under the same applied-field, pressure, and temperature conditions.
measurements: Caloric response (e.g., magnitude of adiabatic temperature change or entropy change under specific field conditions)
Microstructural analysis (to verify tungsten-rich precipitate formation and grain refinement)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in compressive strength (e.g., improvement beyond baseline ± experimental error) or if its caloric performance deviates by more than ±10% from that of the untreated alloy, the hypothesis will be falsified.
